title: 485 strikes and counting: AFCA drops its first non-compliance hit list
full_text:
What happened: AFCA has published its first list naming financial firms that failed to comply with binding determinations.
Who's involved: Dixon Advisory & Superannuation Services, Drive Lah Australia, and 13 other financial firms.
What's at stake: 592 non-compliance reports across the listed firms, with Dixon Advisory accounting for 485 of them.
Why it matters: Every AFCA member, including general insurers, now faces public naming if it ignores a binding ruling.
Where it stands: Published October 1, 2026, under AFCA's new Rule A.11.6 powers.
Four hundred and eighty-five.
That is how many times Dixon Advisory & Superannuation Services has been reported to regulators for failing to honour a binding ruling from Australia's financial complaints authority. The collapsed advisory firm - now in liquidation - accounts for the vast bulk of entries in AFCA's first-ever public naming of firms that ignored its determinations.
The report, published on October 1, 2026, marks the debut of a transparency power AFCA gained under Rule A.11.6, which took effect on March 12, 2026. Under Rule A.18.1(a) of the AFCA Rules, AFCA was already required to notify relevant regulators when firms failed to comply. The new rule goes a step further: it lets AFCA publish those names for the world to see.
Fifteen firms appear across two tables covering sixteen entries - three operating businesses and thirteen under external administration. One firm, Superfast AM Pty Ltd, appears in both. Nearly every entry falls under "Investments." The lone exception is Drive Lah Australia Pty Ltd, a peer-to-peer car-sharing platform that sits under General Insurance - making it the only insurer on the list.
Drive Lah's entry relates to a single case, number 12-25-232809, reported to regulators on May 4, 2026. The report does not disclose the nature of the underlying complaint or the amount at stake.
The scale tips sharply in the administration table. Dixon Advisory's 485 reports dwarf every other entry. United Global Capital Pty Ltd (In Liquidation) sits a distant second with 56. The remaining firms range from one to ten reports each. Where a firm racked up more than five reports, AFCA published only the total rather than individual case numbers - a threshold that hints at the volume behind the headline figure.
AFCA's report carries a pointed caveat: it "does not constitute a finding of misconduct, a breach of law, or regulatory enforcement action." Appearing on this list does not mean a firm broke the law. It means AFCA formed the view that the firm did not follow through on a binding determination within the required timeframe. The report also notes that the information is not updated if a firm later complies.
Before publishing, AFCA says it makes enquiries of the firm and considers the circumstances behind the failure. Publication is not automatic - it is a discretionary step, separate from the mandatory reporting to regulators that has been in place for longer.
Drive Lah's appearance as the sole general insurer is a snapshot, not a clean bill of health for the sector. The rule applies equally to every AFCA member - from major underwriters to niche MGAs to insurtech startups - and the publication framework is ongoing.
For claims and compliance teams at insurers, the practical takeaway is simple: determination deadlines now carry a public consequence. A firm that treats an AFCA ruling as a suggestion rather than an obligation risks landing on a list that brokers, regulators, and competitors will all read.
The AFCA report identifies a failure to give effect to a determination only. It does not constitute a finding of misconduct, a breach of law, or regulatory enforcement action. The information is accurate as at the date of publication and is not updated if a financial firm subsequently gives effect to the determination.
